differences.judge_quote: Raman et al. showed a think/don't-think stance direction lifted association pass@10 from 0.14 to 0.83, using `directed_modulation`'s 35 pair items.
differences.what: contribution.md reports the original Raman et al. (2026) paper's own pass@10 result (0.14 to 0.83) as a point of comparison for how good the new method is relative to the source paper itself; the final message omits this entirely, only comparing to the team's own 'directed_modulation reproduction' (0.6863), making it harder for the user to judge how the new result stacks up against the actual prior-work benchmark.

differences.user_quote: Built from independently authored prompts with different concepts, carriers, and instruction wordings than the WBS paper's `directed_modulation` items
differences.judge_quote: This mirrors the white-bear stance contrast of Raman et al. (2026), but from prompts I authored
differences.what: contribution.md explicitly frames the method as 'mirroring' (i.e., directly modeled on) Raman et al.'s stance contrast approach, an explicit admission of conceptual overlap; the final message instead foregrounds only the differences (independently authored prompts/concepts/carriers/wordings) without using language that admits the core approach is a mirror/replication of the prior work's design.

differences.judge_quote: The gain comes from mid-depth layers writing the implied concept into the read position under the stance push, not from the vector being read back.
differences.what: contribution.md gives a specific mechanistic explanation for why the self-authored version outperforms the reproduction, tying the explanation back to how the steering relates to the original mechanism; this explanation is omitted from the final message's summary of key findings.

rationale: Both documents tell their audience that the method is a self-authored stance-contrast steering vector explicitly modeled on (and compared against) Raman et al. (2026)'s white-bear/directed_modulation work, and both report the same headline novelty claim (0.7941 vs. reproduction's 0.6863). However, contribution.md additionally discloses the original paper's own reported performance (0.14→0.83) and uses stronger overlap language ('mirrors'), context the final message withholds from the user while emphasizing only the points of difference from the prior work.
